Thought Blocks: Non-Autoregressive Latent Communication for Multi-Agent Systems via Trajectory-to-State Compilation

Zhenhan Guan  Xiaolong Liu  Hengwei Ye  Zheng Tian ShanghaiTech University, Shanghai, China AI Lab, The Yangtze River Delta, Changzhou, China {guanzhh2025,liuxl2025,yehw2024}@shanghaitech.edu.cn * Corresponding author: tianzheng@shanghaitech.edu.cn
Abstract

LLM-based multi-agent systems typically communicate through text, incurring repeated generation and re-encoding costs. Although latent communication removes explicit verbalization, constructing latent messages may still require autoregressive latent trajectories. We therefore distinguish message representation from message construction and ask whether agents can directly construct useful continuation states without executing the trajectories that normally produce them. We formulate this problem as trajectory-to-state compilation and introduce Thought Blocks, fixed-size blocks of latent key–value (KV) continuation memory constructed in one shot. Thought Blocks achieve a 2.5×2.5\times average latency speedup over autoregressive latent communication. Compared with text-based multi-agent communication, Thought Blocks reduce text tokens by 45.7%45.7\% and autoregressive steps by 84.8%84.8\%, achieving an 8.6×8.6\times average latency speedup. These results demonstrate that trajectory-to-state compilation enables efficient inter-agent latent communication without sequential latent rollouts at inference.

1 Introduction

LLM-based multi-agent systems have emerged as a promising paradigm for solving complex tasks through decomposition, specialization, and iterative refinement (Li et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2023; Hong et al., 2023; Qian et al., 2024; Du et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023). As these systems are applied to increasingly long-horizon and computation-intensive workflows, communication between agents becomes an important systems concern. For example, OpenAI recently reported using a system of coordinating agents in its work on the Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize Problem, involving approximately 2.7 million inter-agent messages and 130 billion output tokens (OpenAI, 2026). At such scales, the cost of repeatedly constructing and exchanging intermediate information can become a substantial part of multi-agent computation.

Most existing multi-agent systems communicate through natural language (Qian et al., 2024; Yan et al., 2025). Recent latent-communication methods challenge this interface by showing that intermediate information can instead be carried through model-internal representations (Zou et al., 2025; Du et al., 2025; Ramesh and Li, 2025). More importantly, recent mechanistic evidence from the Jacobian Lens identifies a small internal “J-space” in which intermediate results can be retained and reused by subsequent computation (Gurnee et al., 2026). This suggests a separation between the trajectory that produces an intermediate result and the state through which it becomes available to later computation. For inter-agent communication, this motivates a natural hypothesis: a receiver may need only a functionally sufficient continuation state, rather than the sender’s full latent computation trajectory.

This possibility highlights a key distinction: message representation and message construction are separate design choices, and a message can be latent while its construction remains autoregressive. For example, some latent multi-agent protocols eliminate textual messages but still generate a sequence of latent thoughts before transferring the resulting latent state to the next agent (Zou et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026). The communicated object is latent, yet constructing it still requires a sequential latent rollout. We therefore ask: must a useful inter-agent latent state be obtained by executing the trajectory that normally produces it, or can it be constructed directly from the sender’s current state? We formulate this as non-autoregressive latent communication (NALC): constructing inter-agent latent messages without a sequential latent rollout. We call the underlying principle trajectory-to-state compilation: directly constructing the continuation state that the rollout would otherwise produce.

We instantiate this idea with Thought Blocks, fixed-size blocks of latent KV continuation memory constructed in one shot. Our method represents the sender using a factorized continuation state consisting of a compact continuation seed, which indicates how computation should continue, and a context bank, which preserves contextual information that subsequent computation may need to access. A Thought Block writer maps this state directly to an outgoing KV block without autoregressive intermediate-message generation. To train the writer, we use an autoregressive latent teacher to identify useful continuation states and distill these state-level targets into the one-shot writer. The teacher trajectory is therefore used only for supervision during training and is removed entirely from inter-agent message construction at inference time.

Experiments across reasoning and question-answering benchmarks and multiple LLM backbones show that direct continuation-state construction provides a favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-off. Compared with text-based multi-agent communication, Thought Blocks reduce text tokens by 45.7%, autoregressive forward steps by 84.8%, and end-to-end latency by 8.6×\times on average, with an average accuracy difference of only −0.15-0.15 points. More importantly, compared with autoregressive latent communication, where both methods already communicate in latent space, Thought Blocks further reduce autoregressive forward steps by 35.7%, with an average accuracy difference of −0.72-0.72 points. These results provide empirical evidence that useful inter-agent continuation memory need not be constructed by replaying an autoregressive latent trajectory. Our contributions are threefold:

  • •

    We formulate non-autoregressive latent communication as a message-construction problem. We distinguish the representation of an inter-agent message from the process used to construct it, and introduce trajectory-to-state compilation as directly constructing a useful continuation state without executing the trajectory that would normally produce it.

  • •

    We introduce Thought Blocks for one-shot latent communication. Thought Blocks instantiate trajectory-to-state compilation by directly constructing fixed-size KV continuation memory from a factorized sender state and are trained via state-level distillation from autoregressive latent trajectories.

  • •

    We show that autoregressive latent message construction can be substantially reduced while largely preserving downstream utility. Across multiple backbones and diverse reasoning and question-answering tasks, Thought Blocks substantially reduce sequential communication computation, latency, and KV-memory load while maintaining competitive task performance.

2 Related Work

2.1 Efficient Multi-Agent Communication

LLM-based multi-agent frameworks typically coordinate specialized roles through natural-language interaction (Li et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2023; Hong et al., 2023; Qian et al., 2024). Work on communication efficiency reduces this textual overhead through learned communication policies (Chen et al., 2024) or by pruning redundant agents and links (Wang et al., 2025), while retaining natural language as the communication medium.

A complementary line of work communicates through model-internal representations. Activation Communication (AC) exchanges intermediate activations (Ramesh and Li, 2025); InterLat communicates hidden states and studies latent compression (Du et al., 2025); and Thought Communication extracts latent factors for collaboration (Zheng et al., 2025). At the KV-cache level, KVCOMM reuses and adapts KV states across contexts (Ye et al., 2025), KVComm selectively shares informative KV pairs (Shi et al., 2026), C2C projects and fuses source and receiver caches (Fu et al., 2025), and LCF learns compact cache channels (Rossi et al., 2026). StateBridge aligns sender hidden states to the receiver space without training (Peng et al., 2026), while recent work studies heterogeneous KV communication through dense cross-model cache alignment (Chen et al., 2026) and dual-cache transformation  (Liu et al., 2026). Relayed KV memories can also be compressed while preserving task-relevant information (Li et al., 2026).

These methods improve how model-internal states are selected, aligned, transferred, or compressed. In particular, cache-transfer methods primarily operate on sender states that have already been materialized. Our setting instead targets a continuation state that is not yet available at the communication boundary and would ordinarily be reached only after additional latent computation. We ask whether this post-trajectory state can be constructed directly from the pre-trajectory sender state, without executing that trajectory. Accordingly, we use non-autoregressive latent communication to refer specifically to eliminating trajectory-based message construction, rather than broadly to any latent protocol that avoids token-by-token text decoding.

2.2 Latent Trajectories and Direct State Construction

Latent representations do not by themselves eliminate sequential computation. Coconut recurrently feeds hidden states back as continuous inputs (Hao et al., 2024); LatentMAS autoregressively generates latent thoughts before relaying the resulting working memory (Zou et al., 2025); and InterLat’s compressed variant likewise uses recurrent latent computation (Du et al., 2025). Thus, latent messages may still require a sequence of intermediate states to construct.

Other work reduces or reorganizes this sequential structure. PCCoT uses Jacobi iteration to update multiple continuous thought positions in parallel (Wu et al., 2025); CoT2 tracks multiple reasoning alternatives in parallel within each decoding step (Gozeten et al., 2026); and LaDiR constructs latent thought blocks through iterative diffusion-based denoising (Kang et al., 2025). These methods parallelize or iteratively refine latent computation, but inference still instantiates intermediate latent states before the resulting reasoning state becomes available.

We instead ask whether such a trajectory needs to be executed at all when its purpose is to produce a state for another agent. This motivates trajectory-to-state compilation: during training, an autoregressive teacher identifies a useful post-trajectory continuation state, while the student learns to map the pre-trajectory sender state directly to that target. At inference, the teacher rollout is omitted and the outgoing KV continuation memory is constructed in one shot. This separates our work from both transfer or transformation of already-materialized states and methods that accelerate latent trajectory construction. Table 1 summarizes this distinction: Thought Blocks perform inter-agent KV communication by directly constructing a post-trajectory continuation state, without sequential latent rollout or iterative refinement at inference.

3 Method

3.1 Problem Setup

We consider sequential collaboration among NN language-model agents {Ai}i=1N\{A_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}. Given a task qq, each agent AiA_{i} receives a local textual input xix_{i} and, except for the first agent, an inter-agent message ℳi−1\mathcal{M}_{i-1} from its predecessor, with ℳ0=∅\mathcal{M}_{0}=\varnothing. The local input includes the agent’s role instruction and may additionally contain the original task, retrieved evidence, or other observations.

Let 𝒮i\mathcal{S}_{i} denote the sender-side state available after agent AiA_{i} has processed its local input and incoming message. A generic communication step can therefore be written as

𝒮i=Ai​(xi,ℳi−1),ℳi=Γi​(𝒮i),i<N,\mathcal{S}_{i}=A_{i}(x_{i},\mathcal{M}_{i-1}),\qquad\mathcal{M}_{i}=\Gamma_{i}(\mathcal{S}_{i}),\quad i<N, (1)

where Γi\Gamma_{i} denotes the mechanism that constructs the outgoing message from the sender state. The final agent consumes its local input and the last incoming message to produce the task output y^=AN​(xN,ℳN−1)\hat{y}=A_{N}(x_{N},\mathcal{M}_{N-1}). Different communication methods instantiate ℳi\mathcal{M}_{i} and Γi\Gamma_{i} differently. Text-based systems verbalize intermediate computation into natural-language tokens, whereas latent-communication systems expose model-internal states directly. In this work, we represent the communicated object as latent KV continuation memory and focus on a separate question: how should this latent message be constructed?

In trajectory-based latent communication, the outgoing state is obtained by first executing a sequential latent computation,

τi=𝒯θ⋆​(𝒮i),ℳi⋆=Ψθ⋆​(τi),\tau_{i}=\mathcal{T}_{\theta^{\star}}(\mathcal{S}_{i}),\qquad\mathcal{M}_{i}^{\star}=\Psi_{\theta^{\star}}(\tau_{i}), (2)

where τi=(ui,1,…,ui,Tlat)\tau_{i}=(u_{i,1},\ldots,u_{i,T_{\mathrm{lat}}}) is a latent trajectory, 𝒯θ⋆\mathcal{T}_{\theta^{\star}} denotes the sequential latent-computation process, and Ψθ⋆\Psi_{\theta^{\star}} extracts the continuation memory communicated to the next agent. Although ℳi⋆\mathcal{M}_{i}^{\star} is latent, constructing it still requires executing the trajectory τi\tau_{i}. Our goal is to replace this trajectory-dependent construction with a direct parameterized writer,

ℳi=𝒲ϕ;θ⋆​(𝒮i),\mathcal{M}_{i}=\mathcal{W}_{\phi;\theta^{\star}}(\mathcal{S}_{i}), (3)

where ϕ\phi denotes trainable writer parameters and θ⋆\theta^{\star} denotes the frozen language-model backbone. We refer to this replacement of latent-trajectory execution with direct continuation-state construction as trajectory-to-state compilation.

The remainder of this section first specifies the continuation state 𝒮i\mathcal{S}_{i}, then describes how Thought Blocks directly construct an outgoing latent message from this state, and finally explains how this direct mapping is learned from autoregressive trajectories. At inference time, Eq. 3 is applied by each intermediate agent, while the final textual answer is generated through the standard autoregressive language-model interface.

3.2 Factorized Continuation State

Direct continuation construction requires preserving two distinct forms of information available after prefill: a boundary representation that conditions subsequent computation, and addressable prefix memory from which future states can retrieve context. We therefore factorize the sender state as

𝒮i=(Ri,Ci),\mathcal{S}_{i}=(R_{i},C_{i}), (4)

where RiR_{i} is the continuation seed and CiC_{i} is the context bank.

Continuation seed.

Let FF denote the final prefill position after agent AiA_{i} processes its local input xix_{i} together with the incoming latent message ℳi−1\mathcal{M}_{i-1}. We form the continuation seed by stacking the hidden states at this boundary across all LL backbone layers:

Ri=[hi,F1;hi,F2;…;hi,FL]∈ℝL×d,R_{i}=\left[h_{i,F}^{1};h_{i,F}^{2};\ldots;h_{i,F}^{L}\right]\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times d}, (5)

where dd is the hidden dimension. Unlike a final-layer-only readout, RiR_{i} exposes the writer to the full layer-wise representation at the continuation boundary, providing a compact summary from which the outgoing continuation can be constructed.

Context bank.

The boundary representation alone does not provide the addressable prefix memory used by Transformer attention. We therefore retain a compressed KV context bank,

Ci={(Ki,nℓ,Vi,nℓ)}ℓ=1,…,Ln=1,…,NiC,C_{i}=\left\{\left(K_{i,n}^{\ell},V_{i,n}^{\ell}\right)\right\}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\ell=1,\ldots,L\\ n=1,\ldots,N_{i}^{C}\end{subarray}}, (6)

where NiCN_{i}^{C} is the number of retained context positions. Thus, RiR_{i} summarizes the computation at the continuation boundary, while CiC_{i} preserves contextual information in an explicitly retrievable form. This factorization allows the writer to condition continuation construction on RiR_{i} without requiring the seed itself to encode the entire prefix. In our implementation, CiC_{i} is instantiated using Activation Beacon (Zhang et al., 2024). Details of beacon training, compression, and target extraction are provided in Appendix B.1.

3.3 One-Shot Thought Block Writer

Autoregressive continuation uses RiR_{i} and CiC_{i} through a sequential process. Starting from the continuation boundary, each newly generated latent state becomes part of the computation used to construct subsequent states, while the prefix memory remains accessible throughout the rollout. The resulting trajectory therefore performs two functions jointly: it expands the current computational state into future positions and contextualizes those positions using the available prefix memory.

Once the autoregressive rollout is removed, these two functions must be implemented differently. Thought Blocks separate them into parallel continuation expansion and memory-backed rendering.

Parallel continuation expansion.

Autoregressive decoding obtains multiple future positions through temporal recurrence. Without this recurrence, a single continuation seed must instead be expanded directly into multiple latent positions. We introduce BB learnable slots

O=[o1,o2,…,oB]∈ℝB×ds,O=[o_{1},o_{2},\ldots,o_{B}]\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times d_{s}}, (7)

where each slot indexes one position in the outgoing Thought Block. The slots act as position-specific queries over the layer-wise continuation seed RiR_{i}. We construct BB sender-conditioned block embeddings in parallel through a lightweight cross-attention module,

Ei=gϕ​(O,Ri)∈ℝB×d,E_{i}=g_{\phi}(O,R_{i})\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times d}, (8)

where OO provides the queries and RiR_{i} provides the keys and values.

Equation 8 replaces temporal state expansion with parallel positional expansion. Rather than producing future positions through recurrent state transitions, the BB slots query the same continuation boundary simultaneously. Because RiR_{i} contains boundary representations from all backbone layers, different slots can extract different combinations of layer-wise information, yielding distinct sender-conditioned block embeddings without recurrence across block positions.

Importantly, this expansion is intentionally driven by RiR_{i} rather than requiring EiE_{i} to encode the entire preceding context. The role of EiE_{i} is to specify where the computation should continue, not to reproduce everything the model may subsequently need to remember.

Memory-backed rendering.

The expanded block embeddings EiE_{i} specify BB candidate continuation positions, but they do not yet constitute model-native continuation memory. We therefore render them through the frozen backbone while retaining access to the context bank CiC_{i}. Specifically, we treat EiE_{i} as the input embeddings of BB virtual continuation positions and perform a single causal Transformer forward pass. At each layer, the retained keys and values in CiC_{i} are supplied as prefix KV memory, allowing the block positions to retrieve information from the compressed prefix through the backbone’s native self-attention. The complete writer is therefore

ℳi=𝒲ϕ;θ⋆​(Ri,Ci)=Renderθ⋆​(Ei,Ci),Ei=gϕ​(O,Ri),\mathcal{M}_{i}=\mathcal{W}_{\phi;\theta^{\star}}(R_{i},C_{i})=\mathrm{Render}_{\theta^{\star}}(E_{i};C_{i}),\qquad E_{i}=g_{\phi}(O,R_{i}), (9)

where Renderθ⋆\mathrm{Render}_{\theta^{\star}} denotes this single frozen-backbone forward pass. During rendering, the Transformer materializes a key and value at every block position and every layer. We collect these states as the outgoing latent message,

ℳi={(K^i,jℓ,V^i,jℓ)}ℓ=1,…,Lj=1,…,B.\mathcal{M}_{i}=\left\{\left(\widehat{K}_{i,j}^{\ell},\widehat{V}_{i,j}^{\ell}\right)\right\}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\ell=1,\ldots,L\\ j=1,\ldots,B\end{subarray}}. (10)

Although the BB continuation positions interact under the backbone’s standard causal attention mask, they are processed within a single forward pass rather than generated through BB autoregressive decode steps.

3.4 Trajectory-to-State Distillation

Equation 9 specifies how to construct continuation memory directly. We now describe how the writer learns which continuation state to construct.

Teacher state construction.

Starting from the same factorized continuation state (Ri,Ci)(R_{i},C_{i}), the frozen backbone performs autoregressive latent decoding following the continuous latent-feedback interface used in autoregressive latent communication (Zou et al., 2025):

τi=[ui,1,…,ui,Tlat]=ARDecodeθ⋆​(Ri,Ci).\tau_{i}=[u_{i,1},\ldots,u_{i,T_{\mathrm{lat}}}]=\mathrm{ARDecode}_{\theta^{\star}}(R_{i};C_{i}). (11)

The trajectory contains a sequence of intermediate states, whereas the student communicates a fixed-size block. We therefore apply a state-extraction operator Π\Pi to obtain a fixed-size teacher target:

ℳi⋆=Π⁡(τi).\mathcal{M}_{i}^{\star}=\Pi(\tau_{i}). (12)

Importantly, the student is not trained to reproduce the trajectory τi\tau_{i} itself. The trajectory serves only as the computational path through which the teacher reaches ℳi⋆\mathcal{M}_{i}^{\star}. The target of distillation is the resulting continuation state.

Direct continuation-state reconstruction.

The student receives only the pre-trajectory state (Ri,Ci)(R_{i},C_{i}) and directly constructs ℳ^i=𝒲ϕ;θ⋆​(Ri,Ci)\widehat{\mathcal{M}}_{i}=\mathcal{W}_{\phi;\theta^{\star}}(R_{i},C_{i}). Let K^i,jℓ,V^i,jℓ\widehat{K}_{i,j}^{\ell},\widehat{V}_{i,j}^{\ell} denote the student KV states at block position jj and layer ℓ\ell, and let Ki,jℓ,⋆,Vi,jℓ,⋆K_{i,j}^{\ell,\star},V_{i,j}^{\ell,\star} denote the corresponding teacher targets. The primary distillation objective is

ℒKV=1B​L​∑ℓ=1L∑j=1B(‖K^i,jℓ−Ki,jℓ,⋆‖F2+‖V^i,jℓ−Vi,jℓ,⋆‖F2).\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KV}}=\frac{1}{BL}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\sum_{j=1}^{B}\left(\left\|\widehat{K}_{i,j}^{\ell}-K_{i,j}^{\ell,\star}\right\|_{F}^{2}+\left\|\widehat{V}_{i,j}^{\ell}-V_{i,j}^{\ell,\star}\right\|_{F}^{2}\right). (13)

This objective directly matches the representation consumed by the downstream agent. The teacher constructs the target continuation states through sequential latent decoding, whereas the student learns to construct it directly from the continuation boundary state. We additionally use an auxiliary hidden-state alignment objective during training. Because this auxiliary state is neither communicated nor required at inference, its definition is deferred to Appendix B.1. The full objective is

ℒTSD=λKV​ℒKV+λaux​ℒaux.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{TSD}}=\lambda_{\mathrm{KV}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KV}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{aux}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{aux}}. (14)

Only the writer parameters ϕ\phi are optimized during this stage; the language-model backbone and contextual-memory mechanism remain fixed. Trajectory-to-state distillation therefore induces an asymmetric teacher–student computation: the teacher executes a sequential trajectory to reach a useful continuation state, while the student learns the direct mapping (Ri,Ci)⟶ℳ^i.(R_{i},C_{i})\longrightarrow\widehat{\mathcal{M}}_{i}. At inference time, the teacher trajectory and auxiliary training signal are removed entirely.

4 Experiments

4.1 Experimental Setup

Tasks and datasets.

We evaluate on eight datasets spanning three task categories: (1) Science, Commonsense, and Mathematical Reasoning, including ARC (Clark et al., 2018), OpenBookQA (Mihaylov et al., 2018), and GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021); (2) Knowledge-Intensive Question Answering, including MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2021), GPQA (Rein et al., 2024), and MedQA (Jin et al., 2021); and (3) Reading Comprehension, including BoolQ (Clark et al., 2019) and QuAIL (Rogers et al., 2020). We evaluate ARC on both the Challenge and Easy splits and MedQA on its US, Taiwan, and Mainland variants, yielding 11 benchmark configurations in total.

Baselines.

We compare against three baselines. (1) Single-agent: a single model using the same backbone and a matched total decoding budget. (2) Text-based multi-agent (Text-MAS): agents follow the same role decomposition as our method but exchange natural-language messages. (3) Autoregressive latent communication (Latent-MAS): intermediate agents communicate through autoregressively generated latent thoughts (Zou et al., 2025). All multi-agent methods use the same backbone, role decomposition, and number of agents, so they differ primarily in their inter-agent communication mechanism.

Metrics.

We evaluate task utility and inference efficiency, distinguishing end-to-end from communication-stage cost. Task performance is measured by accuracy, using the official evaluation protocol where available and otherwise deterministic exact matching against official gold labels. For end-to-end efficiency, we report text tokens, AR Steps, and latency. Text tokens count the tokenizer-visible input and generated output tokens processed across all agents; AR Steps count autoregressive decoding steps across intermediate communication and final-answer generation; and latency measures wall-clock time for the full pipeline, including prefill, communication, and final decoding.

To capture sequential communication cost not reflected by token counts, we also report communication forward passes (Passes), defined as the number of intermediate-agent forward passes used to construct outgoing messages. Text-MAS and Latent-MAS require sequential passes, whereas Thought Blocks use one non-autoregressive rendering pass per intermediate agent and therefore incur zero autoregressive communication steps. We additionally report KV-cache load, the amount of KV state loaded during decoding. All latency measurements use the same hardware and configuration and implementation details are provided in Appendix B.4.

4.2 Main Results

Table 2 compares Thought Blocks with text-based and autoregressive latent multi-agent communication across four LLM backbones11 1 Full results across all benchmarks are provided in Appendix Table B.1.. Overall, Thought Blocks retain comparable task performance while substantially reducing sequential communication and end-to-end decoding cost. Relative to Latent-MAS, the more direct comparison for isolating message construction in latent space, Thought Blocks reduce communication passes from 1212 to 33 under our four-agent setup (75.0%75.0\%), reduce end-to-end autoregressive steps by 35.7%35.7\% on average, and achieve a 2.5×2.5\times average latency speedup, with an average accuracy difference of −0.72-0.72 points. Relative to Text-MAS, Thought Blocks reduce text tokens by 45.7%45.7\%, communication passes by 99.4%99.4\%, and end-to-end autoregressive steps by 84.8%84.8\%, while achieving an 8.6×8.6\times average latency speedup with an average accuracy difference of only −0.15-0.15 points. Compared with the decoding-budget-matched Single Text baseline, Thought Blocks achieve higher accuracy in all 1212 backbone–category settings, with a +4.25+4.25-point average improvement.

These comparisons separate two sources of communication overhead. Latent communication removes explicit natural-language verbalization, but Latent-MAS still constructs each inter-agent message through a sequential latent rollout. Thought Blocks target this remaining construction cost by replacing the rollout with a single non-autoregressive block-construction pass per inner agent. Under our four-agent setup, this reduces communication-stage passes from 1212 for Latent-MAS to 33 for Thought Blocks; Text-MAS requires hundreds of such passes because its intermediate messages are decoded autoregressively. Notably, Thought Blocks and Latent-MAS have the same macro-average text-token count in Table 2, yet Thought Blocks remain substantially faster. This comparison therefore shows that the efficiency gain is not explained by shorter textual outputs, but by replacing sequential latent message construction with one-shot block construction.

4.3 Ablation Study

We ablate two design choices of Thought Blocks on Qwen3-8B with B=4B=4. First, we test whether the block positions require writer-generated content by replacing the block embeddings EiE_{i} with zero or random vectors while leaving the rest of the pipeline unchanged. Second, we evaluate the factorized continuation state 𝒮i=(Ri,Ci)\mathcal{S}_{i}=(R_{i},C_{i}) by retaining only RiR_{i} or only CiC_{i}.

As shown in Table 3, replacing the writer-generated content of EiE_{i} consistently degrades performance across all eleven benchmark configurations. The average accuracy drops from 79.6479.64 for the full method to 73.4473.44 with Zero-EE (−6.20-6.20 points) and to 71.0671.06 with Random-EE (−8.58-8.58 points). Moreover, Random-EE underperforms Zero-EE on ten of the eleven benchmarks, with an additional average drop of 2.382.38 points. These results rule out the possibility that the gains of Thought Blocks arise merely from introducing additional latent positions. Instead, the content constructed at these positions is functionally important, and replacing it with arbitrary latent values can interfere with downstream computation.

The state-factorization ablations show that both components are important for recovering the performance of the full method. Retaining only RiR_{i} reduces the average accuracy to 61.2861.28 (−18.36-18.36 points), while retaining only CiC_{i} yields 67.1667.16 (−12.48-12.48 points). The CC-only variant outperforms the RR-only variant on all eleven benchmarks, by 5.885.88 points on average, suggesting that the addressable contextual memory carried by CiC_{i} is particularly valuable when each component is considered in isolation. Nevertheless, both single-component variants remain substantially below the full method. This is consistent with the intended factorization: RiR_{i} provides the continuation signal used to construct the block positions, whereas CiC_{i} preserves addressable prefix memory that those positions can retrieve during rendering. Full performance therefore depends on using the two components jointly.

4.4 Effect of Thought Block Size

We investigate how the Thought Block size BB affects the trade-off between communication capacity and efficiency on Qwen3-8B. As shown in Table 4, even B=1B=1 retains substantial task utility, achieving 78.05%78.05\% category-macro average accuracy. Increasing BB to 44 improves accuracy to 81.12%81.12\%, while further increasing it to 3232 yields only modest additional gains, reaching 82.59%82.59\%.

Meanwhile, latency remains nearly constant because all block positions are rendered in a single backbone forward pass, whereas KV-cache load grows with BB. The strong B=1B=1 result is also consistent with our design: each slot is rendered into a full layer-wise KV continuation position conditioned on the compressed context bank. Overall, B=4B=4 provides a favorable balance between accuracy and memory cost.

These results show diminishing returns from increasing the Thought Block size: even B=4B=4 achieves most of the accuracy obtained with larger blocks, while KV-cache load increases approximately linearly with BB. Thus, within the tested range, BB mainly controls the accuracy–memory trade-off rather than acting as a highly performance-sensitive hyperparameter.

4.5 Decoding-Time KV-Cache Load

Table 5 reports decoding-time KV-cache load. Thought Blocks load 8.35 MB on average, compared with 58.29 MB for Latent-MAS and 71.13 MB for Text-MAS, reducing loaded KV-cache volume by 85.7% and 88.3%, respectively. This shows that the efficiency gain extends beyond token count and sequential forward steps to substantially lower decoding-time KV-cache load.

5 Discussion and Limitations

Our results support a distinction between message representation and message construction. Thought Blocks show that useful continuation states can be constructed directly from the sender state without executing an autoregressive latent rollout at inference, while preserving comparable downstream utility across multiple backbones and tasks. This suggests that autoregression is one mechanism for reaching a useful latent state, rather than an intrinsic requirement of latent communication. The results nevertheless reflect an accuracy–efficiency trade-off: performance varies across tasks and models, and larger blocks provide diminishing accuracy gains at increasing KV-memory cost.

Our study focuses on establishing whether autoregressive latent message construction can be compiled into a direct continuation-state mapping. The current training pipeline uses autoregressive teacher rollouts to provide offline state-level supervision, but this sequential computation is removed entirely at inference. Consequently, the additional training cost is a one-time overhead whose importance depends on deployment scale; our amortization analysis in Appendix B.3 suggests that it becomes relatively small in sufficiently high-volume multi-agent workloads. We evaluate this principle in controlled sequential, shared-backbone systems in order to isolate message-construction effects. Extending direct state construction to heterogeneous backbones, richer communication graphs, and long-horizon tool-using agents is an important direction for future work. Finally, latent KV messages are not directly human-readable, so applications requiring auditable intermediate artifacts may benefit from hybrid protocols that selectively externalize text while using one-shot latent communication on internal, high-frequency communication edges. More broadly, we view Thought Blocks not as a universal replacement for text or sequential reasoning, but as an efficient communication primitive that can be deployed selectively when intermediate trajectories need not themselves be exposed.

Appendix A Method Overview

Appendix B Experiment Setups

B.1 Training Thought Blocks

Training follows the same trajectory-to-state view introduced in Sec. 3.4. Stage I trains the Activation Beacon mechanism used to instantiate the compressed context bank while keeping the language-model backbone fixed. Stage II then performs trajectory-to-state distillation. Starting from the factorized continuation state 𝒮i=(Ri,Ci)\mathcal{S}_{i}=(R_{i},C_{i}), a frozen autoregressive latent teacher executes the trajectory τi\tau_{i} and a state-extraction operator Π\Pi converts that trajectory into a fixed-size teacher continuation-memory target ℳi⋆\mathcal{M}_{i}^{\star}. The one-shot Thought Block writer receives only (Ri,Ci)(R_{i},C_{i}) and is trained to reconstruct this target directly. The teacher trajectory is therefore used only to construct supervision during training and is removed entirely at inference time.

B.1.1 Stage I: Beacon Training

We instantiate the context bank CiC_{i} with Activation Beacon (Zhang et al., 2024). Let θ\theta denote the backbone parameters and let β\beta denote the trainable Beacon mechanism, including the Beacon embedding and Beacon-specific projections. Given a training corpus 𝒟\mathcal{D}, we optimize only β\beta with the Activation Beacon objective,

β⋆=arg⁡minβ​𝔼x∼𝒟​[ℒAB​(Beaconβ​(x),θ)].\beta^{\star}=\arg\min_{\beta}\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}\left[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{AB}}\bigl(\mathrm{Beacon}_{\beta}(x);\theta\bigr)\right]. (15)

The language-model weights are not updated in this stage. We use θ⋆\theta^{\star} to denote this frozen backbone in the remainder of the paper and freeze the trained Beacon mechanism β⋆\beta^{\star} as well. Consequently, Stage II optimizes only the writer parameters ϕ\phi, including learnable slots OO.

B.1.2 Stage II-A: Teacher State Construction

For each training example xix_{i}, we first run the same Beacon-compressed prefill used by the main method to obtain the pre-trajectory continuation state

𝒮i=(Ri,Ci),\mathcal{S}_{i}=(R_{i},C_{i}), (16)

where RiR_{i} is the layer-wise continuation seed at the final prefill position and CiC_{i} is the compressed, addressable prefix KV memory defined in Sec. 3.2.

The frozen backbone then performs autoregressive latent decoding from this state. Following autoregressive latent communication (Zou et al., 2025), the last-layer teacher hidden state is mapped back to the model input-embedding space before being used as the next continuous input. Under the row-vector convention, we use the fixed alignment operator

Wa=Wout†​Win∈ℝd×d,W_{a}=W_{\mathrm{out}}^{\dagger}W_{\mathrm{in}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}, (17)

where Win,Wout∈ℝ|𝒱|×dW_{\mathrm{in}},W_{\mathrm{out}}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|\times d} are the backbone input- and output-embedding matrices and Wout†W_{\mathrm{out}}^{\dagger} is the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse. If hi,tteachh^{\mathrm{teach}}_{i,t} is the last-layer teacher hidden state at latent step tt, the continuous latent state used by the next step is

ui,t=hi,tteach​Wa.u_{i,t}=h^{\mathrm{teach}}_{i,t}W_{a}. (18)

The resulting teacher trajectory is exactly the trajectory used in the main text,

τi=[ui,1,…,ui,Tlat]=ARDecodeθ⋆​(Ri,Ci).\tau_{i}=[u_{i,1},\ldots,u_{i,T_{\mathrm{lat}}}]=\mathrm{ARDecode}_{\theta^{\star}}(R_{i};C_{i}). (19)

To instantiate the state-extraction operator Π\Pi in Eq. 12, we insert decode-stage Beacons along the teacher rollout and retain the states at the BB valid Beacon positions. The extracted teacher continuation-memory target is

ℳi⋆=Π⁡(τi)={(Ki,jℓ,⋆,Vi,jℓ,⋆)}ℓ=1,…,Lj=1,…,B.\mathcal{M}_{i}^{\star}=\Pi(\tau_{i})=\left\{\left(K_{i,j}^{\ell,\star},V_{i,j}^{\ell,\star}\right)\right\}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\ell=1,\ldots,L\\ j=1,\ldots,B\end{subarray}}. (20)

At the same retained positions, we additionally record the corresponding last-layer hidden states

Zi⋆={zi,j⋆}j=1B,Z_{i}^{\star}=\left\{z_{i,j}^{\star}\right\}_{j=1}^{B}, (21)

which are used only for the auxiliary training loss and are not part of the communicated message. Thus, each collected supervision record contains (Ri,Ci,ℳi⋆,Zi⋆)(R_{i},C_{i},\mathcal{M}_{i}^{\star},Z_{i}^{\star}). This construction makes the distillation target model-native: the writer learns to reconstruct continuation states actually reached by the frozen autoregressive teacher rather than arbitrary latent tensors.

B.1.3 Stage II-B: Thought Block Writer Training

Given (Ri,Ci)(R_{i},C_{i}), the writer first performs the same parallel continuation expansion as in Sec. 3.3,

Ei=gϕ​(O,Ri),E_{i}=g_{\phi}(O,R_{i}), (22)

and then renders the BB virtual continuation positions through the frozen backbone conditioned on CiC_{i},

ℳ^i=Renderθ⋆​(Ei,Ci).\widehat{\mathcal{M}}_{i}=\mathrm{Render}_{\theta^{\star}}(E_{i};C_{i}). (23)

The same forward pass also produces the last-layer hidden states used by the auxiliary objective. We denote them by

Z^i={z^i,j}j=1B,ℳ^i={(K^i,jℓ,V^i,jℓ)}ℓ=1,…,Lj=1,…,B.\widehat{Z}_{i}=\left\{\hat{z}_{i,j}\right\}_{j=1}^{B},\qquad\widehat{\mathcal{M}}_{i}=\left\{\left(\widehat{K}_{i,j}^{\ell},\widehat{V}_{i,j}^{\ell}\right)\right\}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\ell=1,\ldots,L\\ j=1,\ldots,B\end{subarray}}. (24)

The primary objective is the same KV-state reconstruction loss defined in Eq. 13,

ℒKV=1B​L​∑ℓ=1L∑j=1B(‖K^i,jℓ−Ki,jℓ,⋆‖F2+‖V^i,jℓ−Vi,jℓ,⋆‖F2).\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KV}}=\frac{1}{BL}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\sum_{j=1}^{B}\left(\left\|\widehat{K}_{i,j}^{\ell}-K_{i,j}^{\ell,\star}\right\|_{F}^{2}+\left\|\widehat{V}_{i,j}^{\ell}-V_{i,j}^{\ell,\star}\right\|_{F}^{2}\right). (25)

The auxiliary hidden-state alignment objective deferred from the main text is

ℒaux=1B​∑j=1B‖z^i,j−zi,j⋆‖22.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{aux}}=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{j=1}^{B}\left\|\hat{z}_{i,j}-z_{i,j}^{\star}\right\|_{2}^{2}. (26)

The complete trajectory-to-state distillation objective is therefore

ℒTSD=λKV​ℒKV+λaux​ℒaux,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{TSD}}=\lambda_{\mathrm{KV}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KV}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{aux}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{aux}}, (27)

which matches Eq. 14. Only ϕ\phi is updated in Stage II; θ⋆\theta^{\star} and β⋆\beta^{\star} remain frozen. At inference time, neither the autoregressive teacher trajectory τi\tau_{i} nor the auxiliary target Zi⋆Z_{i}^{\star} is needed: the writer directly applies (Ri,Ci)↦ℳi(R_{i},C_{i})\mapsto\mathcal{M}_{i} in one forward pass.

B.3 Full Experiment Results

Amortized Efficiency at Scale.

Fig. B.2 compares the cumulative token and latency cost of Thought Blocks against autoregressive latent MAS on Qwen3-8B. The x-axis denotes the number of task instances under our default four-agent setting. Although Thought Blocks introduce an additional one-time training cost, this cost is fixed with respect to deployment volume, whereas the inference savings accumulate over every subsequent multi-agent call. Under this setting, our method becomes more token-efficient after approximately 8.82×1048.82\times 10^{4} task instances and faster after approximately 3.37×1053.37\times 10^{5} task instances.

These crossover points should be interpreted as conservative for more communication-intensive workflows. Our experiments use four agents per task. If a task requires more agents, more communication rounds, or richer inter-agent state transfer, the per-instance saving from removing autoregressive latent rollout increases, while the one-time training cost remains unchanged. Therefore, the amortization point would move earlier as the amount of inter-agent communication per task grows.

The task counts required for amortization may appear large in a standalone benchmark setting, but they are modest in shared deployment scenarios. General-purpose AI systems already serve hundreds of millions of weekly users, and recent enterprise surveys report rapidly growing experimentation with AI agents (Bellan, 2025; McKinsey & Company, 2025). We do not assume that current deployments exactly match our experimental setting. Rather, these trends suggest that the cost of inter-agent communication will become increasingly important as agentic systems move from small closed multi-agent teams toward higher-volume services and cross-agent interactions, where agents may need to represent different users, tools, or organizations. In such settings, reducing both sequential inference cost and communication memory traffic can translate into substantial aggregate savings.

B.4 Implementation Details

Hardware Environment.

All experiments are conducted on a server running CentOS Linux 7. The server is equipped with two Intel Xeon Gold 6430 CPUs and eight NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPUs with 48 GB memory each. Unless otherwise specified, Writer training and latency evaluation use a single visible GPU rather than distributed data-parallel execution.

Beacon Backbone Training.

We build the compressed-context backbone following Activation Beacon (Zhang et al., 2024) and follow the original configuration without modification. During Beacon training, the language-model backbone is frozen and only the Beacon parameters are optimized, including the Beacon embedding and the Beacon-specific query, key, and value projections. Beacon positions are interleaved with the original tokens; both the sliding window and stride are set to 2,048 tokens, with full-coverage attention and access to previous Beacon states.

Beacon training consists of pretraining followed by long-context fine-tuning. For pretraining, we follow the Activation Beacon recipe based on the RedPajama-Data-1T-Sample corpus. Each document is terminated with an EOS token and documents are not packed together. Only the Beacon-specific parameters are optimized during this stage.

For long-context fine-tuning, we use a data mixture, consisting of GPT-generated long-document QA from books and papers, LongAlpaca, BookSum, synthetic needle-retrieval data, and a 5K-example RedPajama subset. We use a maximum sequence length of 8,192 tokens, a minimum sequence length of 1,024 tokens, one fine-tuning epoch, a learning rate of 1×10−51\times 10^{-5}, bf16 precision, FlashAttention-2, and DeepSpeed ZeRO-2.

Teacher State Construction.

The pre-trajectory continuation state is constructed using the same state representation as in the main method: earlier groups retain only Beacon KV states, while the final group keeps its raw-token KV states, and the layer-wise hidden states at the final prefill position form the continuation seed.

For trajectory-to-state supervision, the frozen teacher performs autoregressive latent decoding from the pre-trajectory state (Ri,Ci)(R_{i},C_{i}). The teacher rollout follows a fixed decoding horizon, capped at 12 decode steps under the standard configuration, with an extended 96-step configuration used only for larger slot-count studies. Decode-stage Beacons are placed along the resulting trajectory.

After constructing the teacher rollout, the state-extraction operator Π\Pi converts the fixed-horizon latent trajectory into a fixed-size teacher continuation-memory target ℳi⋆\mathcal{M}_{i}^{\star}, represented by BB Beacon states. Here, BB denotes the size of the distilled continuation-memory representation rather than a truncation of the teacher rollout.

The retained states are model-native continuation states reached along the teacher’s autoregressive latent trajectory. The Thought Block writer is trained to directly reconstruct the corresponding continuation-memory target from (Ri,Ci)(R_{i},C_{i}), replacing the sequential autoregressive construction of these states with a fixed-size one-shot prediction. The teacher trajectory is therefore required only for constructing supervision during training and is removed at inference time.

Thought Block Writer Training.

The language-model backbone and Beacon mechanism remain frozen throughout this stage, and only the Writer parameters ϕ\phi are optimized. Our standard configuration uses B=4B=4 learnable slots and a Beacon compression ratio of r=2r=2. For each teacher rollout, we collect the valid decode-stage Beacon states in their causal order and retain the BB such states as the fixed-size continuation-memory target ℳi⋆\mathcal{M}_{i}^{\star}. Importantly, the block size BB determines the number of retained Beacon states rather than the length of the teacher rollout. The teacher decoding horizon is configured to provide sufficient valid Beacon positions for the corresponding block size. Writer training is performed purely through latent-state distillation.

We train the Writer with AdamW for 10 epochs using a learning rate of 5×10−55\times 10^{-5}, weight decay of 10−210^{-2}, gradient clipping at 1.0, and dropout 0. The training loss combines KV-state matching and the auxiliary hidden-state alignment defined in Eq. 26, with weights λKV=1.0\lambda_{\mathrm{KV}}=1.0 and λaux=0.5\lambda_{\mathrm{aux}}=0.5, respectively.

The mixed teacher-trace dataset contains 78,207 valid training examples. We use a batch size of 8, corresponding to 9,776 optimization steps per epoch. The training examples consist of synthetic data and the training splits of the benchmarks, including ARC-Easy, BoolQ, GSM8K, GPQA, MedQA-US, MedQA-Mainland, MedQA-Taiwan, MMLU, OpenBookQA, and QuAIL. Each training example records the role prompt, the pre-trajectory continuation representation, and the hidden/KV states associated with decode-stage Beacon positions. All reported benchmark results are evaluated on the evaluation/test splits, and no test-split teacher traces are used for Writer training.

Latency and Efficiency Measurement.

End-to-end latency is measured sample-by-sample with an effective inference batch size of 1. The timer covers the complete multi-agent inference pipeline, from the first agent’s initial prefill to completion of the final output, including prompt construction, tokenization, model forward passes, inter-agent state-transfer logic, and final decoding. We measure host-observed wall-clock time using time.perf_counter and report the total elapsed time divided by the number of evaluated samples as the average per-sample latency. We call torch.cuda.synchronize() immediately before starting and after completing each timed inference to ensure that all queued CUDA kernels are included in the wall-clock measurement.

The reported KV-cache load is computed analytically from the corresponding KV tensors using their shapes, element sizes, and data types. It is therefore a memory-volume proxy rather than a hardware-profiler measurement of actual PCIe or HBM traffic.
